Human Rights. Moral and legal entitlements believed to belong to all people simply by virtue of their humanity, independent of social status, national origin, or circumstance. The philosophical concept emerged from Enlightenment thinking about natural rights and the intrinsic dignity of rational persons. Modern human rights frameworks—international treaties, declarations, constitutional law—attempt to protect basic freedoms: conscience, expression, assembly, equality, and freedom from torture, enslavement, and discrimination.

Natural rights theory, developed by philosophers like Locke and Rousseau, claims that humans possess inherent rights—life, liberty, and property—that precede government. Governments do not create these rights; they must protect them. Kant grounded rights in human dignity. Rational beings have inherent worth that demands respect, he argued, and cannot be treated as mere means to others' ends. The Enlightenment's emphasis on universal reason led to claims that rights belong to all humans equally. This challenged existing hierarchies of privilege and caste.

The United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted in 1948, attempted to forge a global consensus on fundamental human entitlements. Yet rights can conflict. Free speech can clash with protection from harassment. The precise scope of rights remains philosophically and politically debated. Philosophers distinguish negative rights—freedom from interference—from positive rights, which are entitlements to assistance or resources. Healthcare, education, and shelter are positive rights.

Contemporary debates explore universal human rights versus cultural relativism. Are rights grounded in objective truths about human nature and dignity? Or do rights claims reflect Western cultural values imposed globally? This remains one of the most challenging questions in political and moral philosophy. It affects how the international community responds to human rights abuses and how diverse societies negotiate conflicting values.
